area.dimension_description: Area here means a characteristic area under explicit qualifiers, often a surface area, cross-section, footprint, or geographic extent. Mixing those notions blindly would be misleading, so each entry states what kind of area is being used. The point is coverage across scales, not a claim that all areas answer the same question.
area.name: Area

units.description: Square meters are the canonical storage unit for all area observations.
units.name: square meters

units.description: Square centimeters are useful for small surfaces and cross-sections.
units.name: square centimeters

units.description: Square kilometers are useful for geography and astronomy.
units.name: square kilometers

units.description: Hectares are common for land area and agriculture.
units.name: hectares

units.description: Acres are widely used in land records and real estate.
units.name: acres

density.dimension_description: Density is mass per unit volume under stated composition, temperature, and pressure assumptions. Most entries below are bulk average densities rather than microscopic local densities, and extreme astrophysical entries are explicitly marked when they refer to stellar cores or degenerate matter.
density.name: Density

units.description: Kilograms per cubic meter are the canonical storage unit for density.
units.name: kilograms per cubic meter

units.description: Grams per cubic centimeter are common in chemistry and materials science.
units.name: grams per cubic centimeter

frequency.dimension_description: Frequency measures how often something repeats per second, from once-per-cosmic-era cycles to electromagnetic radiation oscillating millions of trillions of times each second. Some entries here are direct oscillation frequencies, while others are derived from a reported period using frequency = 1 / period. That makes this dimension especially useful for connecting rotations, rhythms, waves, resonance, and light on a single logarithmic axis.
frequency.name: Frequency

units.description: Hertz are cycles per second and the canonical storage unit for frequency.
units.name: hertz

units.description: Microhertz are useful for very slow astronomical or geological cycles.
units.name: microhertz

mass.dimension_description: Mass tracks inertia and the amount of matter under a stated definition, from subatomic particles to galaxies. Some entries are direct measurements, while others are derived estimates such as the mass of a lake from its volume and density. Every item names the object and the measurement basis so the scale remains comparable.
mass.name: Mass

units.description: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass. All canonical mass values in this dataset are stored in kilograms before conversion.
units.name: kilograms

units.description: Grams are convenient for laboratory and everyday masses.
units.name: grams

units.description: Milligrams make very small biological and chemical masses readable.
units.name: milligrams

units.description: Metric tons are useful for vehicles, buildings, and cargo.
units.name: metric tons

units.description: Earth masses are convenient for planetary comparisons.
units.name: earth masses

units.description: Solar masses are convenient for stars, galaxies, and cosmology.
units.name: solar masses

volume.dimension_description: Volume tracks three-dimensional extent under explicit geometric assumptions. Many values here are derived from a stated radius, diameter, or envelope shape rather than directly measured container capacity. Each item therefore includes a short qualifier describing whether it is a literal volume, an effective occupied volume, or an approximate geometric envelope.
volume.name: Volume

units.description: Cubic meters are the canonical storage unit for volume.
units.name: cubic meters

units.description: Liters are convenient for household and laboratory volumes.
units.name: liters

units.description: Milliliters are useful for droplets, teaspoons, and lab samples.
units.name: milliliters

units.description: Cubic kilometers are convenient for lakes, planets, and nebulae.
units.name: cubic kilometers
